evidence: Cic. Off. 1.89: mediocritātem illam tenēbit, quae est inter nimium et parum (Lewis & Short, s.v. nimius)
terms.comment: The neuter of nimius as a noun, with a genitive: aurī argentīque nimium, too much gold and silver. Proverbially nē quid nimis, “nothing in excess” (Ter. And. 61). For “too, too much” as an adverb, see too-excessively.

evidence: Cic. Tusc. 4.22: omnium perturbātiōnum fontem esse dīcunt intemperantiam (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Excess in conduct: in eating, drinking, desire, speech (linguae, Tac. Ann. 4.18). Also arrogance towards others.

evidence: Cic. Sull. 30: efferrī immoderātiōne verbōrum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Rare (Lewis & Short); the adjective immoderātus and Traupman’s immodicus (excessive, Traupman 152) are commoner.

phrases.latin: apprīmē in vītā esse ūtile ut nē quid nimis
phrases.english: that the most useful thing in life is nothing in excess

phrases.latin: mediocritātem illam tenēbit, quae est inter nimium et parum
phrases.english: he will keep to that mean which lies between too much and too little

sources: Lewis & Short: nimius · Lewis & Short: intemperantia · Lewis & Short: immoderatio · Lewis & Short: immodicus
Terence from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-terentius); the other passages as Lewis & Short quotes them.
